posts.text:
I spent some time this week reading ERP Today's coverage of SAP Connect, and what stayed with me wasn't a product name but a number: 110,000. That's how many SAP employees are already using Joule Work internally, and the company says it's seeing roughly 20% productivity gains across finance, HR and procurement. I find the fact that SAP is dogfooding at that scale more persuasive than any slide full of agent logos.

What Joule Work actually seems to be is a natural-language layer sitting on top of the SAP Knowledge Graph — reportedly more than 7 million data fields — so you can ask a question across systems instead of hopping between transactions. One customer, Maschinenfabrik Reinhausen, described work that used to take up to an hour now taking seconds. I'm wary of hero anecdotes, so I'd want to know how typical that is before assuming the average looks like the best case.

The part that keeps me honest: the finance-specific assistants — revenue recognition, disclosure — aren't shipping now. They're flagged for early adopters in Q1 2027. So the headline is here, the finance substance is next year. My guess is that gap is where the real learning happens, not in the keynote.

Worth a read if SAP sits in your stack: https://erp.today/at-sap-connect-sap-expands-joule-across-every-line-of-business/

The SAP Connect announcements are easier to judge if you separate what's measured from what's promised. On the measured side, per ERP Today: 110,000 SAP employees now using Joule Work, about 20% internal productivity gains across finance, HR and procurement, and a 50% cut in trade-classification effort in early International Trade Assistant deployments. Those are internal or early-customer numbers — real, but not yet independently generalisable.

On the promised side sits most of the finance value. The revenue recognition and disclosure assistants are slated for Q1 2027 early adopters; spend analytics and the customer-experience assistants land in roughly the same window. So the shape of the roadmap is: horizontal infrastructure now, line-of-business finance depth in about twelve months.

The figure I'd anchor on is 20%. If it holds outside SAP's own walls it's material — but productivity measured by the vendor, on the vendor's own staff, is the friendliest possible test. My read is that the honest planning assumption is a fraction of 20% in year one, scaling only as the Knowledge Graph grounding (7M+ fields) actually maps onto your data. The technology looks credible; the timeline is the thing to plan around.

Source: https://erp.today/at-sap-connect-sap-expands-joule-across-every-line-of-business/

One detail from the SAP Connect coverage stuck with me more than the headline figures: Joule Work is grounded in the SAP Knowledge Graph, reportedly more than 7 million data fields. It isn't a flashy number, but it may be the one that matters. The reason natural-language queries tend to fall apart in enterprise systems is almost never the language model — it's that the model doesn't know what a given field means in your particular configuration. Grounding is the unglamorous plumbing that quietly decides whether any of this works.

Widen out and the same theme repeats. Nestlé is piloting an Accounts Receivable assistant on S/4HANA across 140 countries; the value there isn't clever conversation, it's consistency over messy, multi-jurisdiction data. SAP says 110,000 of its own staff use Joule Work with roughly 20% productivity gains — a figure I'd treat as a ceiling rather than a forecast, since it's the vendor measuring itself.

What I take from ERP Today's write-up is that the agent era in ERP will be won or lost on data grounding, not model cleverness. The companies whose master data is already in order will get something near that 20%. Everyone else gets a very articulate assistant confidently answering the wrong question.
